D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b000_.text: Every potluck I ever went to had the same first plate empty. 60 years in church basements, honey, and the deviled eggs went first every single time. Nobody could ever tell me why. Well, I can tell you why, and it takes two minutes. Pull up a chair and sit with me. If you watched my last one, the pot roast, you know I like to find the thing everybody does wrong. Today, it is a plate of deviled eggs. Everybody boils the eggs, peels them, mashes the yolks, and dumps the mayonnaise straight in. Then the filling comes out lumpy and a little flat, and the plate still goes first. Today, I'll show you the one step almost nobody takes, and I'll walk you through the whole recipe from page 20 of my little cookbook, every amount, so you can make it at your own table. Let me tell you about the first time I brought deviled eggs to a funeral lunch.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b001_.text: I was 22 years old and Harold's mother handed me a platter and said, fill these for the family. I made them the way my own mother did, mashing the yolks and stirring the mayonnaise right in. They looked fine on the platter. But when I came back to the table, every yolk had a little gray ring around it and the filling was lumpy like cold oatmeal. Nobody said a word, they just left them sitting there. You know that feeling, don't you? You worked all morning and you can tell it didn't come out right. So here is what we are going to do. We cook the eggs the church way, 12 minutes at a low boil, then straight into a bowl of ice water. We peel them without tearing the whites. Then comes the trick, the one that turns a plate of eggs into the plate that empties first. We season the yolks before any mayonnaise goes near them and we let them sit for two minutes. That's it.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b002_.text: It takes about 25 minutes of work, a little waiting, and you will understand every single step because I'll tell you why each one matters. Let me take you back to the church basement where I cooked for 60 years. Along the wall there was one long cold table and it was the table where you could tell whose kitchen was whose. Somebody's green salad, somebody's macaroni salad that tasted like the basement itself, and my deviled eggs at the end near the coffee urn. 200 people came through that line on a funeral day. The eggs were gone in 10 minutes. The ladies who ran that table learned their little tricks the way you learn to ride a bicycle, by falling off a few times and getting back on. My mother had a rule about the egg carrier and I still keep it. The egg carrier never leaves the cook's hands until the plate is on the table.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b003_.text: She said a dish that travels in somebody else's arms comes out lopsided. She would walk into a church supper with that plastic carrier held out in front of her like a crown, and nobody was allowed to touch it, not even the pastor. I didn't understand the rule when I was young. I understand it now. A plate of eggs is delicate, and so is a good cook's pride. So here are the three things people get wrong with deviled eggs. First, they buy eggs straight from the store and try to peel them the same day, and the whites tear into little pieces. Second, they boil them too hard for too long, and the yolk turns that gray -green color that looks like pond water. Third, and this is the big one, they stir the mayonnaise into the yolks right away before the yolks have a chance to take any seasoning. Fix those three things, and you have the best plate at the potluck. One more thing before we move on.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b004_.text: In my cookbook, every recipe gets a little mark that tells you what it costs per serving. This one gets the cheapest mark there is, which means pennies a serving. Eggs, a spoon of mustard, a splash of pickle juice, and a little mayonnaise. Nothing fancy, and nothing you have to drive across town to find. Here is what goes in, and I'll say each amount slowly. 12 large eggs, a week old if you can get them. Two teaspoons of yellow mustard, one tablespoon of dill pickle juice, one teaspoon of sugar, half a teaspoon of salt, a quarter teaspoon of black pepper, half a cup of mayonnaise, and paprika, and a little chopped dill for the top. 12 eggs make 24 halves, honey, which is a nice plate for a small supper. Step one is the water. Bring a pot of water to a gentle boil, then lower the eggs in with a big spoon so they don't crack against the bottom.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b005_.text: Cook them 12 minutes at a low boil, not a rolling boil, a low one, with little bubbles coming up around the eggs. The reason is simple. A low boil cooks the white all the way through without turning the yolk gray, and that is the whole secret of a yellow yolk you could eat by itself. Step two is the bowl of ice water. Move the eggs straight from the pot into a big bowl of ice water and let them sit there for 10 minutes. Don't leave them in the hot water while you go check your phone. The cold shock stops the cooking the moment it's done, and it helps the shell come off clean. If you skip the ice and let them cool slowly on the counter, you get that gray -green ring I was telling you about. That ring is the cooking going on too long, and it only takes a minute to stop it. Step three is peeling. Crack each egg all over gently on the counter.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b006_.text: Then peel it under a thin stream of cold water, starting at the wide end, which is where the air pocket is. The water gets under the shell and lifts it right off. If your eggs are fresh from the hen, they will fight you and you'll end up with pitted whites. That is why I told you to buy them a week ahead. Old eggs peel easy and the whites stay smooth for the pretty platter. Step 4 is cutting. Take a sharp knife and dip it in water, then cut each egg in half, lengthwise, from the top to the bottom. Keep the blade wet between cuts so the yolks stay in the middle where they belong. Pop the yolks out into a bowl and set the whites on a plate, cut side up. Look at them, 12 eggs, 24 little white boats. Now the yolks are the only thing that matters for the next few minutes. Step 5 is the mashing. Take a fork and mash the yolks fine until there are no lumps left at all.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b007_.text: Then stir in the mustard, the pickle juice, the sugar, the salt and the pepper. You want a stiff yellow paste, the color of a school bus, and it should smell like pickles and mustard before a single spoon of mayonnaise touches it. Why do it this way? Because the cooked yolk is dry and thirsty. It will soak up the seasoning and it can't do that once it's buried under mayonnaise. And now comes the trick, the one I've been waiting to tell you about. Leave it alone for two minutes. Set a timer on the stove or just count slow, the way I count stitches. Don't add anything. Don't stir. Just let that paste drink in the mustard and the pickle juice. Two minutes is all it takes. The yolk drinks the seasoning and the flavor goes all the way through instead of just sitting on the top.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b008_.text: Most people skip this part because they are in a hurry and that is the reason their filling tastes like plain mayonnaise. After the two minutes, stir in the half cup of mayonnaise until the filling is smooth and creamy with no streaks in it. Then spoon it into the whites or pipe it if you have a bag and make a nice little mound. Dust each one with paprika and add a few pieces of chopped dill on top for the color. Cover them and chill them until serving time. When you lift one out, you'll see how silky the filling is. That is the trick working honey, I want you to see this on paper, so here it is. This is page 20 of my little cookbook, The Church Pot Luck Deviled Eggs, with the ingredients on the left and my method down the middle. You'll see the trick written right there, in the box, just the way I said it. Season the yolks first, then wait two minutes.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b009_.text: Every amount is on the page, so you don't have to guess at a single thing when you're standing at your own counter. So that's the whole recipe, from the water to the paprika. It is on page 20 of my little cookbook and the link to the book is right under this video. Those 50 recipes are the ones I carried up the basement stairs for 60 years, written the way I'd tell them to you standing beside you. Take a look when you have a minute and make the eggs for your family this week. Now let's talk about the mistakes because I made every one of them. The first is the eggs that won't peel. That is almost always eggs that are too fresh, so buy them a week ahead. The second is the gray -green ring on the yolk and that comes from overcooking or from letting the eggs cool slowly. 12 minutes at a low boil and straight into ice water and that ring will never show up at your table.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b010_.text: The third mistake is the lumpy filling, and it happens when the mayonnaise goes in first. Mash and season the yolks before any mayonnaise, and you'll never have lumps again. Let me tell you about my grandson Danny. He's the one who sat me down at the kitchen table and said, Grandma, write it down before it's gone. He grew up eating these eggs at every church supper, and he still asks for them at Easter, with his fingers already reaching for the platter. When he was little, he used to stand guard by the egg carrier, just like my mother taught me. He'd say, Grandma, nobody touched the eggs. Then he'd snitch one anyway, and I'd pretend I didn't see it. Those are the moments I think about when I'm cooking now. Now, if you're cooking for a crowd, here is how I do it. Two dozen eggs make 48 halves, which is enough for a supper of about 40 people.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b011_.text: When you are taking them to the church or the family reunion, carry the egg whites and the filling in separate containers. Fill the whites right there at the table, just before people come through the line. That way the whites stay smooth and the filling stays cold and nobody gets a soggy egg on a hot afternoon. And if you are cooking for one or two, which I am too, since Harold passed, here is the small version. Make four eggs, which gives you eight halves. Use a third of everything else, the same trick, the same two minutes. The filling keeps two days in the refrigerator, covered, so you can have a little plate of eggs with your supper on Tuesday and another on Thursday. Nobody has to throw away half a dozen eggs they didn't need. Keeping them is simple honey, but it matters. Put the eggs in the refrigerator, covered, for up to two days.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b012_.text: and never leave them out of the cold for more than two hours. That is the same rule I wrote on page nine for every cold dish, and I'd rather you follow it than throw out a whole platter. If your potluck runs long on a warm afternoon, set the platter in a bowl of ice and take the eggs back into the cooler when the line goes quiet. Sometimes you wanna change it up a little, and that's fine. For ham and egg, stir a quarter cup of finely chopped ham into the filling after the mayonnaise. For a sweet pickle taste, use sweet pickle juice instead of the dill and add a tablespoon of sweet relish. The trick stays the same no matter what you add. Season the yolks first, then give them two minutes, then the mayonnaise. You can make them your own once you know why each step is there. My friend Bernice always stood at the end of that cold table watching the eggs disappear.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b013_.text: One Easter, she said to me, Loretta, you are going to have to make more eggs than the men can eat. I said, Bernice, nobody can eat that many eggs. She was right, of course. By the end of the morning, the men were back for seconds and Bernice was taking a plate home for her husband. That's the kind of thing you remember for 60 years. Cooking is a way of saying you thought about somebody. Now I know some of you are watching on a tablet or a phone with a cookbook close by. If you want the page, point your phone at the little square on the screen. That is the code for the book. It takes you right to the recipe and you don't have to write down a single thing. Go ahead and try it when you're ready. I'll wait right here and then we'll finish the rest together. If you liked this one, you might enjoy another video from my kitchen, the 10 One Pan Suppers for Seniors Living Alone.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b014_.text: Harold's been gone nine years, and the first year I cooked for two and threw half of it away. Those suppers taught me how to make a small pan of food that tastes like a church supper without the leftovers piling up in the refrigerator. You'll find it on this channel, and I think you'll find a supper in it you like. I learned something from every funeral I cooked for, and I cooked for over 900 of them. When a family is grieving, they don't need a fancy dish. They need something they can count on, something that goes on the table without a fuss. The deviled eggs were always that dish. People would walk past the big casseroles and reach for the eggs because they tasted like home. That is the point of the whole recipe, honey. It's not about showing off. It's about feeding people who need to be fed. Now, your first batch may look a little rough, and that's just fine.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b015_.text: Mine did too, for years. Maybe a yolk gets a gray tinge because the water boiled too hard or a white tears on the first egg. Eat that one yourself honey and make the second batch better. A church cook never got it right on the first try. She got it right by the 10th tray and by then everybody was asking for her recipe. So let's go over it one more time because I like to say things twice in my old age. 12 eggs in a gentle boil, 12 minutes. Straight into ice water for 10 minutes. Peel under cold water from the wide end. Halve them and pop the yolks out. Mash the yolks, then season them with the mustard, the pickle juice, the sugar, the salt and the pepper. Leave them alone for two minutes. Then the mayonnaise, the paprika and the dill. Chill them and serve them cold. That's the whole thing. When you've made these for your family, I want you to take a plate to somebody.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b016_.text: That's what the recipes were for in the first place. And if you want the rest of the 50, the link to the cookbook is right under this video and page 20 is where the eggs are. 49 more church supper recipes, one page each, with the trick written right there so you don't have to remember it at 10 o 'clock at night. Next week, I'm going to show you the candied sweet potatoes every church lady brought to Thanksgiving. I'll tell you why you should never boil them first and why the syrup slides right off when you do. Don't miss it. You'll be sitting right here with me and I'll have the coffee on. Now, here is my question for you and I read every comment myself. What is the first dish that disappears at your table? Tell me in the comments and tell me who made it.

D:\\wt\\ckeggs\\vlog\\ckeggs\\voz\\b017_.text: I love hearing about the cooks behind the dishes, the way I love hearing about the people in the church basement who kept me going all those years. Thank you for sitting with me today, honey. Go on and cook something for somebody you love. May your eggs peel clean, your yolks stay soft and seasoned, and may there be a plate or two left for the people who come late. God bless you, and God bless your table.
